title: Split your email list three ways
metaTitle: Email list segmentation for IT firms
description: If clients and cold leads get the same email, one of them is getting the wrong one. Three segments, and one extra email a month for people mid-deal.
dek: Split the list into clients, people mid-deal and everyone else. Three types are fine, and the middle one matters most.
author: Shane Kennedy

video.title: Split your list. Marketing for IT firms

images.alt: “One list? Wrong email” in bold capitals, beside a woman holding out a letter

shortVersion: If clients and cold leads get the same email, one of them is getting the wrong one.
With one list, clients can get pitched and people mid-deal get general news. The people closest to buying get the least relevant email you send.
Give the people in a conversation with you one extra email a month, tied to what they asked about.

beats.heading: One newsletter for everyone
body: If you run a newsletter, there's often one list and one email for everyone.
As the list grows, the people on it have less and less in common.

beats.heading: Clients get pitched
body: That can mean current customers get pitches, or people mid-deal get general news.
So the people closest to buying get the least relevant email you send. Someone who's asked for a quote this week gets the same company news as someone who downloaded a guide two years ago.

graphic.eyebrow: One email for the whole list

beats.heading: Three segments are fine
body: The answer is proper segmentation in your CRM. Three types are fine.
Clients, those in a conversation or a deal cycle, and then everyone else.
In practice that's three tags. If you've met someone, sent them a quote, or they've told you "not yet", they're in the middle group.

items.title: In a conversation
items.text: Met, quoted, or in a deal cycle

beats.heading: One extra email for the middle group
body: That middle group is the most important one. They should get an extra email every month, tied to what they asked about.

Keep it short and about their question. If they've asked what a cloud migration would cost, send them the questions that decide the price, and if they've asked about security, send them the checklist you'd run on their network first.

right.title: The extra email
rows: Goes to people in a conversation
Tied to what they asked about

take.line: That one extra email per month is the one that will get your deals
body: Set up the three tags this week, and write the first extra email for whoever's in the middle group now.
Nurture is part of Centurion, the strategy we run with IT firms.
